title: The board arrives: solder it, prove it
summary: Solder the fabricated board, power it up, hunt down the first fault with the multimeter if it does not work, and compare it against the perfboard twin.
materials: the fabricated PCB ordered in week 3
the components it needs (LED, resistor, switch)
soldering iron kit and safety glasses

steps.title: Ask, imagine, plan
steps.body:
The design loop closes the loop it opened in week 2: ask, imagine, plan, build, test, fix.

Ask: does a machine-made board actually work the same as the hand-soldered one that already proved the circuit?

Imagine: the real board, silent and untested, until solder and power turn it into a working circuit for the first time.

Plan: lay the schematic next to the board before soldering anything. Mark where each component goes. Decide which two or three points you will check with the multimeter first if the board does not light up right away.

figure.alt: A row of four boxes, power, switch, resistor and LED, connected by short wires with three numbered test points marked along the connections. A caption explains that the fault sits wherever the expected reading first disappears when checking the points in order, 1 then 2 then 3, from power outward.

items.s: Trace point by point from power outward
Fault sits where the expected reading first disappears

steps.title: Test it before you trust it
steps.body:
A board that does not work the instant it is powered is not rare, it is normal. The useful question is never did it work, it is where did it stop working.

With the schematic in hand, the multimeter can trace a circuit the same way it traced the perfboard's joints in week 3. Check for a solid connection where the schematic says one should exist. Check for voltage where the schematic says power should reach.

Start at the power connection and work outward toward the LED, checking one point at a time. The first place the expected reading disappears is usually where the fault sits. That might be a joint that never truly soldered, or a part placed the wrong way round.

figure.alt: The fabricated board's switch, resistor and LED wired in a row and soldered. A multimeter wired in series below the circuit, breaking into the loop to read milliamps, measures the current once the board is powered, so it can be compared with the perfboard twin's current from week 3.

items.s: Solder the fabricated board, then measure its current
Compare current with the perfboard twin from week 3

steps.title: Solder, power up, find the fault
steps.body:
With an adult, solder the components onto the fabricated board, following the schematic. Take your time with each joint rather than rushing to see it light up.

Power it up. If it works first try, that is real, but do not skip the multimeter check anyway. If it does not, trace the circuit point by point from the power connection outward. Compare each reading with what the schematic predicts, until you find where the expected reading disappears.

Once it works, measure the current it draws with the multimeter in series, and compare that number with the same measurement taken on the perfboard twin from week 3.
checklist: An adult was present for the entire soldering step
Components were placed by checking the schematic, not by copying the perfboard photo
If the board did not work first try, the fault was traced point by point with the multimeter
Current was measured on both the fabricated board and the perfboard twin

steps.title: Fabricated board versus perfboard twin
steps.body:
The circuit, the components and the power source stay the same for every row. Only which board is being measured changes.

Measure each board's current three times, six rows in total. For each run, write which board it was and the current the multimeter read in milliamps.
steps.question: Did the fabricated board draw about the same current as the perfboard twin, and what was the gap in milliamps?

steps.title: Bug diary
steps.body:
One line for each thing that did not work the first time and what you tried. Classics this week: a component soldered facing the wrong way, since a fabricated board's silkscreen marks are easy to misread the first time.

Also watch for a joint that looks fine but is actually cold. And watch for a current reading that is far off the perfboard's, which usually means the fault trace stopped one point too early.

steps.title: Show it
steps.prompt: Photo of the fabricated board working next to the perfboard twin, with the multimeter reading current on one of them, and your six-row table

extras.title: Design a two-fault test board
extras.body:
Starting question: could you build a small circuit with one fault hidden inside it on purpose, then trace it with the multimeter the same way you traced today's board?

Constraints: it must use parts already on hand from the electronics kit. The fault must be something the multimeter can actually detect, such as a missing connection or a part placed backward. Nobody but you knows where the fault is until it is found.

Sketch the schematic first, mark the hidden fault on your own copy only, then build it and hand the working schematic to a family member to trace.

How to know it works: the family member finds the fault using only the multimeter and the schematic, the same method used on the real board today.
